To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) we have identified a CAM-independent adhesion process involving BMs that is essential for the structural integrity of embryonic NMJs in Drosophlia; and (b) we have shown that loss of all classical cadherin, neurexin, or GluR adhesion factors in Drosophilia, or combinations between these, does not lead to detectable structural phenotypes at NMJs.

(i) loss of all neuxins, all classical Cadherins or all Laminins fails to reveal structural phenoytypes in the Drosophla embryonic NMJ, and (ii) loss of type IV collagen, or of Laminin A causes detachment of motorneurons from the muscle surface.

(i) loss of all neuxins, all classical adhersins or all glutamatergic receptors, as well (ii) as combinations between these factors or with Laminin deficiency fail to reveal ultrastructural defects at the Drosophil NMJ.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular and structural underpinnings of synaptic junctions, which are the key to the understanding of the development and maintenance of synapses, and the basis for the emergence of brain function.
the fundamental question of how synapses are built, and how they can maintain their structure and function over time.
understanding the molecular and cellular processes that underpin synapse formation, and the role of adhesion in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CAMs are dispensable for the structural integrity of synapses at the Drosopila NMJ, while BMs are essential for it.
, in the absence of a loss-of-function phenotype, it cannot be concluded that a CAM does not contribute to synaptic adhesion.
, at the embryonic Drosophila NMJ, CAMs are not required for the structural integrity of synaptic adhesion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BMs provide structural support to the NMJ, and that CAMs provide functional support.
BM-dependent mechanisms and CAM-independent adhesion are essential for the structural support of synapses.
the NMJ of Drosophla embryos is a robust system, in which adhesion molecules are buffered and redundant, but the BM is essential for structural support.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the NMJ is a complex synapse that relies on a multitude of adhesion factors to form and maintain its structure, and that the loss of individual factors is unlikely to result in a detectable structural phenotype.
the structural role of CAMs at synapses is more subtle than expected.
the synaptic adhesion mechanisms at this model synapses appear more complex than previously thought.
